intro: Think about a house. Before the builders lay a single brick, someone draws a plan: where the walls go, where the pipes run, which rooms sit next to each other. That plan is hard to change later. Moving a wall is easy on paper and very expensive once the house is built. **Software architecture** is the plan of a program. It is the set of big decisions that give the program its shape and that cost a lot to change afterwards.

Most programs start small and grow. If nobody thinks about the shape, the code turns into a tangled ball of string: pull one thread and ten others move. A good architecture keeps the pieces separate, so a change in one place does not break the others. This matters in real life every day. It is why a shop can change its payment company without rewriting the whole website, and why a phone app can work with one database today and another tomorrow.

In this summary you will learn what architecture is and how we judge it, then a family of styles that answer one question: how do we keep the **business rules** (the rules that make the program useful, like "a cart total is the sum of its items") safe from the **details** (the database, the web framework, the screen)? You will meet layers, the hexagon, the clean architecture and its dependency rule, one program against many small services, events, and the vocabulary of domain-driven design. At the end you will see why every choice is a trade-off, and how teams write their decisions down.

sections.title: What architecture is and quality attributes

blocks.text: Imagine you build a toy city with blocks. Some choices are cheap to undo: the colour of one roof. Other choices are expensive: where the main road goes, because every house is placed around it. In software, the **architecture** is made of the expensive choices. Authors such as Martin Fowler and Ralph Johnson describe it as the set of design decisions that matter, the ones that are hard to change. It also lives in the shared understanding of the team, not only in a document.

Robert Martin adds that there is no clear line between architecture and detailed design. The small decisions hold up the big ones, so it is one continuum. He also says what the goal is: to **minimise the people and effort needed to build and maintain the system**. A good architecture keeps the cost of each new change low during the whole life of the program. One way to do that is to keep options open, which means not choosing a detail too early.
Architecture = the decisions that give the system its shape and are expensive to change. Its goal is to keep the cost of change low.
Functional and non-functional requirements

A **functional requirement** says what the program does, such as "a customer can place an order". A **non-functional requirement** says how well it does it: how fast, how often it is up, how safe, how easy to change. Individual parts implement the functions, but the non-functional properties depend on the architecture as a whole. This is why two online stores with the same buttons can need very different architectures: one for 50 users in an office, another for 5 million users around the world that must be up 99.99% of the time.
Quality attributes need a measurable scenario

A **quality attribute** is a word like performance, availability, security or maintainability. "The system must be fast" is not useful, because no test can fail it. A good requirement is a **scenario**: under which condition, which response is measured, and what the limit is. For example: "with 1,000 users at once, 95 out of 100 searches answer in under 300 milliseconds". It describes the result we want, not the technical solution.

headers: What it asks of the structure
rows: Critical work kept in a few large parts that talk to each other as little as possible
Layers, with the most valuable data in the innermost one
Redundancy: spare copies that take over when one part fails
Small parts that are easy to replace
blocks.caption: Each attribute pulls the structure in a different direction (after Sommerville)

blocks.text: Look at the table: performance wants few big parts, maintainability wants many small ones. They pull in opposite directions, so an architecture is always a **compromise** between the attributes that matter most for that system.
Information hiding

David Parnas had a simple idea in the 1970s: split the program into modules so that **each module hides one decision that is likely to change**, like how the data is stored. Other modules only know a small, stable interface (the list of things the module offers). Then, when the decision changes, the change stays inside one module. If six files read the same global list of orders and expect it sorted by date, changing that list breaks six files. That is the opposite of hiding.
Views, folders and teams

One drawing cannot show everything. Kruchten's **4+1 view model** uses four views: **logical** (the key ideas), **process** (what runs at the same time), **development** (the modules the programmers handle) and **physical** (which machines run what). The "+1" is a set of **scenarios** that ties the four together. The view about processors and machines is the physical one.

Robert Martin also talks about a **screaming architecture**. The plan of a library building "screams" that it is a library. In the same way, the top folders of a program should scream what the program does (orders, payments), not which framework it uses. If the folders say only `controllers`, `models` and `views`, the framework is deciding the shape.

blocks.content:
Screams the framework      Screams the business

src/                       src/
  controllers/               orders/
  models/                    payments/
  views/                     shipping/
  helpers/                   catalogue/
blocks.caption: Two ways to name the top folders

blocks.text: **Conway's law** (1968) says that organisations build systems whose structure copies how the organisation talks. Three teams writing a compiler tend to make a compiler with three passes. It describes what usually happens, it is not a design rule. The **inverse Conway manoeuvre** uses it on purpose: first arrange the teams the way you want the architecture, then let them build it. Drawing new services on paper while keeping the old teams usually brings back the old split under new names.
A diagram does not change a system. If the teams and the way they talk stay the same, the code will follow the teams, not the diagram.

Think of a school. The pupil asks the teacher, the teacher asks the secretary, and the secretary looks in the archive. Nobody jumps from the pupil straight to the archive. That is the **layered architecture**: the program is cut into levels, from the closest to the user down to the closest to the data. Each layer offers services to the layer above it and uses only the services of the layer just below. Because of that, a layer can be replaced without disturbing the others, as long as its interface stays the same.

blocks.caption: Three layers: calls go only downward

blocks.text: Layer and tier are different words

A **layer** is a logical division: a group of code with one job, like "presentation". A **tier** is a physical division: where the code runs, for example the browser, the application server and the database server. You can have three layers running on a single machine, or two layers spread over five machines. The two counts do not depend on each other.
Strict and relaxed layering

In **strict (closed) layering** a layer calls only the layer right below it. This isolates changes, but sometimes a layer has methods whose only job is to pass the call on. In **relaxed (open) layering** a layer may call any layer below it. That removes the useless forwarding, but raises **coupling** (how much one part depends on another), because more layers now depend on the same lower layer.

When most requests cross a layer that does nothing but forward them, we call it the **sinkhole anti-pattern** (an anti-pattern is a common bad habit). A few such cases are normal. When they are the majority, rethink the layers or open some of them, accepting the extra coupling.
Hexagonal architecture: ports and adapters

Alistair Cockburn had another picture. Think of a laptop with sockets on its sides. The laptop does not care what you plug in, as long as the plug fits the socket. In the **hexagonal architecture** (also called **ports and adapters**) the application is at the centre. It knows only **ports**: interfaces that the application itself declares, saying what it needs or what it offers. Each outside technology connects through an **adapter**, a piece that translates between the port and the technology. The word port here has nothing to do with network ports.

blocks.content:
HTTP controller --+              +-- PostgreSQL adapter
  Command line   ---+--> [PORT] <--+
  Automated test ---+  APPLICATION +-- In-memory adapter

  driving adapters            driven adapters
  (start the call)            (are called)
blocks.caption: The application only sees ports. Adapters plug in from outside

blocks.text: Why a hexagon? Only because it is a shape with many sides. Cockburn wanted to show many equivalent ports, with no "top" and "bottom" as in the layers picture. What matters is the difference between the **inside** (the application) and the **outside** (the adapters).

rows: The outside world calls the application
HTTP controller, command-line tool, an automated test
The application calls the outside through a port it declared
blocks.caption: The criterion is who starts the call

blocks.text: A port can have many adapters: the real database, one that keeps data in memory, a test double. Since the application depends only on the port, the adapter is chosen from outside. So the business rules can be tested without a database, and the real adapter is tested separately.
The big difference from classic layers

In the three classic layers, dependencies point downward, so the business layer depends on persistence and ends up shaped by the database. In the hexagonal architecture the core declares the port, and persistence implements it. The **calls** still go from the core to the database, but the **source-code dependency** points toward the core.

blocks.caption: Who imports whom

blocks.text: Ivar Jacobson's **BCE** pattern has the same spirit with three kinds of object: **boundary** (talks to the actors outside), **control** (coordinates the steps of one use case) and **entity** (holds data and rules of the domain). It is one of the influences of the clean architecture, together with the hexagonal one and DCI: entity matches entities, control matches use cases, boundary matches interface adapters. If the class that reads the HTTP request also holds the sequence of the flow, it mixes boundary and control.
Layers: calls go down. Hexagon: the application declares ports and the outside plugs adapters into them, so the dependency points at the core.

sections.title: Clean architecture and the dependency rule

blocks.text: Picture an onion. In the middle lies the most precious part, and each skin around it protects it. Robert Martin's **clean architecture** draws the program as circles inside circles. From the centre outward: **entities** (the most general business rules), **use cases** (rules of this particular application), **interface adapters** (controllers, presenters, repositories) and, outside, **frameworks and drivers** (the web framework, the database, the tools). The further in, the higher the level of the policy.

blocks.caption: The four circles. The number of circles is only an illustration

blocks.text: A system does not need exactly four circles. They are a drawing, not a requirement. What defines clean architecture is the dependency rule below.
The dependency rule

The **dependency rule** says: **source-code dependencies point only inward**. Code in an inner circle knows no name from an outer circle, not a class, not a function, not a type. As a result, the business rules do not change when you swap the database or the web framework.

Martin calls the database and the web **details**. They are ways to bring data in, send it out and store it, but they are not the reason the system exists. The rules are at the centre, and the details connect from the outside, like plug-ins. This lets you postpone and replace them. It also gives the main characteristics Martin lists: independence of frameworks, of the user interface and of the database, and rules that can be tested without any of them.

Being independent of frameworks does not mean never using one. It means the business rules do not depend on it. The framework stays in the outermost circle and is treated as a tool. Also, the outer code changes often and the inner code rarely, and because dependencies point inward, the thing that changes often depends on the thing that changes rarely, never the other way round.
Calls go out, dependencies go in

Here is the puzzle. A use case must save a note in the database, so at run time it calls code in an outer circle. Does this break the rule? No, because **the flow of control and the source-code dependency are different things**. The solution is **dependency inversion** (the D of SOLID, a set of five design principles). The use case declares an interface of its own, the **port** `NoteRepository`. The outer class `PostgresNoteRepository` implements it. So the call goes outward, but the source code dependency points inward.

blocks.content:
Order of calls at run time:
  NoteController
    -> CreateNote
    -> PostgresNoteRepository
    -> database

Where each name is declared:
  adapters/   NoteController
  use-cases/  CreateNote, NoteRepository (interface)
  drivers/    PostgresNoteRepository (implements it)
blocks.caption: Control goes out, but each import points inward

rows: A principle: high-level code and low-level code both depend on an abstraction
[[Dependency injection|an object receives what it needs from outside, usually in the constructor]]
A mechanism that delivers the real object to the one that needs it
An optional tool that creates and connects objects automatically
blocks.caption: Three words that are often mixed up

blocks.text: Finding a violation

To check the rule, read the `import` lines of each file and compare the layer of the importer with the layer of the imported. Importing something further in is allowed, even skipping circles. Importing something further out is the violation. A type is a name too. In TypeScript an `import type` vanishes when compiled, but the coupling stays in the source, because a change in the outer type breaks the inner file. Outer names can also hide without an import line: the global `Response` type or an HTTP status code in a use case already ties it to the web.

blocks.caption: The second import breaks the rule

blocks.text: Because the rule is about source code, a machine can check it without running the program. A script or a lint rule maps each folder to a layer and rejects any import from an inner layer to an outer one. Run in the build or in continuous integration (the automatic checks on every change), it stops the violation before the code is merged.

Clean architecture is not a silver bullet. It shrinks the part of a change that reaches the rules, but writing a new adapter or migrating data is still work. It does not ask for an interface for every class: abstractions have a cost, and they pay off at the boundaries between circles. In small, throwaway programs the extra cost may not be worth it.

Think of a restaurant. Some rules belong to the food itself: a salad has a vegetable in it. Other rules belong to how this restaurant works: orders are taken in this order, then the kitchen is told. The first kind lives in the **entities**, the second in the **use cases**.

In clean architecture, the **entity** sits in the innermost circle and holds the most general business rules, the ones that would hold even if the work were done by hand on paper. It depends on no database, framework or screen. For that reason it changes little and can serve more than one application of the same company. A **use case** (also called an **interactor**) holds a rule that is specific to the application: the sequence of steps of one operation, such as "create a note". It orchestrates the entities and reaches the database, the clock or the network only through ports that it declares itself. It does not know who calls it, or where the data is stored.

rows: A title cannot be empty or longer than 80 characters
A user cannot have two notes with the same title
No, it looks at the object alone
Often yes: it checks the notes already stored
blocks.caption: Where does a rule go? Ask: would it hold in another application built on the same concept?

blocks.text: Entities keep the closed rules that define the concept. A rule that is a decision of one product, that may still change, or that needs to look at other stored data goes in a use case. Then the entity stays reusable and the rule remains easy to find in the application code. Protocol, pagination and tables are details of outer layers, not rules at all.
Value objects that cannot be wrong

A **value object** is a small object defined only by its values, like a `Title`. If its constructor is **private** and the only way in is a factory method `create`, then nobody can build an invalid one. Whoever receives a `Title` as a parameter can trust it, and the rule is written in a single place. The invalid state becomes impossible to represent.

blocks.caption: A self-validating value object

blocks.text: Notice that `create` returns a **Result** (also called Either): either a success with the value or a failure with an error. Expected errors, like a bad title, are part of the contract of the operation, so a Result shows them in the signature and forces the caller to decide what to do. **Exceptions** are kept for failures nobody expected, like a database that is down.
The anemic domain model

Martin Fowler named an anti-pattern: the **anemic domain model**. The domain classes only hold data, and all the rules live in separate procedural services around them. The central idea of object orientation, keeping data and rules together, is lost. The usual result is duplicated rules and objects that can end up in an invalid state.
What crosses the boundary

The input and the output of a use case are simple data structures, with no behaviour, defined by the use case layer itself. The controller turns the request into that input, and the presenter turns the output into what the screen needs. That way neither the framework nor the entity leaks to the other side. A use case also should not know if it was called by HTTP, a command line or a test: it returns a result in application terms, and each adapter translates it. Status codes, SQL and `console.log` do not belong in it.
Ports for time and randomness

The current time and random values change at every run. Code that reads them directly (`new Date()`, `crypto.randomUUID()`) is not **deterministic**: it does not give the same answer for the same input. So the use case receives an `IdGenerator` and a `Clock` as ports. In tests we hand it fixed versions, in production the real ones, and the use case never changes.

A port belongs to the code that uses it. That is why `NoteRepository` is declared next to the use cases, and `PostgresNoteRepository` implements it in an outer layer. A test of `CreateNote` can then use an in-memory repository, a fake clock and a fake id generator, with no server and no database. It runs in milliseconds and checks the application rule alone. SQL, routes and wiring are checked by the tests of each adapter.
Entity: the closed rule that defines the concept. Use case: the steps of this application, using ports for everything outside.

When you travel to another country, you may carry a plug adapter, so your charger fits a different wall socket. The **interface adapters** layer does the same job for data. It sits between the use cases and the outside world and converts data from the form that is best for use cases and entities into the form that is best for the web or the database, and back. Controllers, presenters and gateways live here.

request -> Controller -> input data -> Use case
                                           |
                                      output data
                                           v
screen  <- View <- view model <- Presenter
blocks.caption: A controller on the way in, a presenter on the way out

Decide business rules, touch the database, know display details
Turns the output of the use case into a view model: formatted texts, flags, labels
Decide what the business rule is
Copies the view model values to the screen or terminal
Translates between storage format and entities
Be imported by the use case
blocks.caption: Who does what

blocks.text: A good controller is **thin**: it is simple to test and simple to replace. The same use case output can have different presenters, for example one for HTTP and another for the command line.
The humble object

Some code is hard to test, like drawing pixels on a screen. The **Humble Object** pattern splits the behaviour in two. The hard-to-test part goes into a "humble" object with as little logic as possible. Everything else goes into an ordinary object that is easy to test. In clean architecture the **view** is the humble object, and the **presenter** is the testable part. Because the presenter already prepared every text and flag, the view only copies them.
Keeping the framework out

If the controller received the context object of the web framework, the adapters layer would depend on a detail of the outer layer. Instead, the adapters declare plain request and response types. The framework converts its own context to them and calls the controller. The controller can then be tested with plain object literals. For the same reason, neither the framework request nor a database row is passed inward: that would make the inner layer know something about the outer one. The controller picks out the fields and builds the input structure.

blocks.caption: Plain types declared in the adapters layer

blocks.text: Translating errors

A use case says what happened with a domain or application error, and names no protocol. For example, `RemoveNote` returns `NoteNotFound`. Deciding that this means HTTP status 404 is the adapter's work: invalid input becomes 400, a missing resource becomes 404, an unexpected failure becomes 500. A command-line adapter would translate the same errors into other things, like a message and an exit code.
Two kinds of validation

There are two checks, and they live in different places. **Syntactic validation** asks if the outside input has the expected shape: are the fields there, are the types right? It happens at the boundary, where a schema library like Zod can be used. **Business validation** protects the invariants of the domain, for example that a title is not blank and has at most 80 characters. It lives in entities and value objects, so it holds on every input path, not just through the web.
Where does the repository live?

The interface `NoteRepository` belongs to the use-case layer, which defines what it needs. The implementation is an adapter. In the layering presented by Otávio Lemos, an adapter that talks directly to a driver or an external library, such as the PostgreSQL client, is placed in the outermost layer, where importing the library is allowed. The interface adapters layer is then left free of external dependencies. The use case must never import the adapter file, that is the flaw to avoid.
Controllers and presenters translate. Validate the shape at the edge and the business meaning in the domain. The view is humble.

sections.title: Frameworks, drivers and the composition root

blocks.text: In a house, the walls and rooms are the plan, but the electric sockets, the taps and the paint are things you can change. The outermost circle of clean architecture holds these replaceable things: the web framework, the database driver, the input and output libraries, and the small glue code that connects them to the adapters. Usually little code of your own is written there. Martin calls this circle **details**, because nothing in it defines what the system does, only how it is delivered and stored.

He advises keeping the framework "at arm's length". A framework is written by people who do not know your problem and have no commitment to it. If your entities and use cases extend the framework's base classes, the commitment goes one way: your code depends on the framework, and a new version or a replacement means rewriting the centre. Kept at the edge, behind adapters, the framework is used without the system marrying it.
The composition root

Someone has to create the real objects and plug them together. Think of the electrician who connects everything in a new house: he must know all the rooms, but no room needs to know him. This place is the **composition root** (Martin calls it **Main**). It is the entry point of the program, the dirtiest and outermost component. It knows every layer and every tool, so **nothing may depend on it**. Concentrating the assembly in one place lets the rest of the code depend only on abstractions.

blocks.content:
main/ (composition root)
  reads config
  new PostgresNoteRepository(url) --+
  new UuidGenerator()             --+--> new CreateNote(...)
  new SystemClock()               --+
  hands the ready object to the entry points
blocks.caption: The composition root builds the object graph once

blocks.text: Constructor injection

With **constructor injection**, a class says what it needs in its constructor and receives a ready object. If a class instead creates its dependency with `new`, or fetches it from a **service locator** (a global shelf where objects are looked up), it is stuck with one implementation and hides that link from the people who use it. With injection, the dependency is visible in the signature and can be replaced in tests.

blocks.caption: Two ways a use case can get its repository

blocks.text: The swap experiment

A good test of the whole design: add a new class `SqliteNoteRepository` that implements the port. Which existing code must change so the application runs with it? If everything inside depends on ports and the assembly is in factories of the composition root, the answer is only the composition root: a factory reads the configuration at start-up and chooses the implementation. If another file has to change, there is undue coupling somewhere.
Configuration and secrets

Environment variables, like `MAX_NOTES`, are a detail of the runtime environment. So they are read at the edge, by the composition root, which validates and converts them once and passes them inward as plain values through constructors. The inner layers never touch `process.env`, and a test configures a use case just by passing another number.

Configuration that changes per environment, and above all **secrets** such as a database password, stays out of the code and out of the repository. The real `.env` file is listed in `.gitignore`. A file like `.env.example` is committed, with the variable names and obviously fake values. A newcomer then knows what to configure, and no credential stays in the history.
ORMs

An **ORM** (object-relational mapper) is a tool that converts table rows into objects. It is a persistence detail and belongs at the edge. Decorators on the entity, or an entity that inherits from an ORM class (the **Active Record** style), make the centre depend on the tool. The compatible alternative is the **Data Mapper** style: a separate schema in the outer layer, and a repository that translates between rows and entities.
Only the composition root names concrete classes. Everything else receives ports through the constructor.

A **monolith** is like a big lunch box: everything is in one box, and you carry it all together. In software, a monolith is a system delivered as a **single deployable unit** (one thing you release as a whole). The word is about how the system is packaged and released, not how the code is organised inside. So a monolith can be well organised, and a group of services can be a mess.

A **microservice** is a service that can be deployed on its own, owns its data and is built around one business capability, such as payments or catalogue. Its size in lines of code is not part of the definition. The useful question is: **can I change and release this service without asking the others?**

rows: Each service has its own database
Network calls, which can fail or be slow
Simplicity, easy changes at the start
The costs of a distributed system
blocks.caption: A quick comparison

blocks.text: Database per service

If two services read and write the same tables, the database schema becomes a contract between them that nobody wrote down. Any structural change has to be agreed and released together, and that cancels independent deployment. This is why each service keeps its own data and shows it to others only through its API or through events.
Modular monolith and distributed monolith

The **modular monolith** has a single deployment with strong boundaries inside: each module is a business area, exposes a public interface and does not let others reach its details. It gives much of the order of microservices without the cost of a distributed system. If a service must be taken out one day, the boundary already exists.

The opposite mistake is the **distributed monolith**. The system was cut into services, but they are still tightly tied: they must be released together, share a database or form long chains of synchronous calls. It has the problems of both worlds. A practical test: can one service be released alone? If every release needs all six services at once, in a fixed order, it is a distributed monolith.
Monolith first

The advice associated with Martin Fowler is to **start with a monolith**. At the beginning of a product nobody knows yet where the right boundaries are. In a monolith, fixing a wrong boundary is a local refactoring (reorganising code without changing what it does). Between services, the same fix means changing network contracts, migrating data and coordinating releases.
Cut by business, not by layer

Services should be cut by **business capability** (or bounded context), not by technical layer. A feature usually touches every layer: a field in the form, a rule, a column. If the services are `ui`, `business-logic` and `data-access`, one feature changes three services and three teams. If they are `catalogue`, `ordering` and `payment`, what changes together stays together.

blocks.content:
By layer (bad)              By business (better)

  ui-service                  catalogue-service
  business-logic-service      ordering-service
  data-access-service         payment-service
                              shipping-service
blocks.caption: Two ways of cutting the same shop

blocks.text: The network is not a function call

A local call finishes or fails together with its caller. A network call has a third result: **unknown**. If a request times out, maybe the other side did the work and only the answer was lost. This is **partial failure**, and "the network is reliable" is one of the classic fallacies of distributed systems. Retrying blindly can charge a card twice. The defence is to make the operation **idempotent** (doing it twice has the same effect as once), for example by sending an **idempotency key** on every attempt.

Chains of synchronous calls also hurt availability, because the request needs every service at the same time, so the availabilities are multiplied. With each service up 99% of the time and independent failures:

blocks.title: Availability of a chain of synchronous calls

blocks.text: For three services the math is 0.99 x 0.99 x 0.99 = 0.970299, about 97.03%. To avoid long chains, teams use asynchronous communication, caching or degraded answers.
Sagas

Placing an order must reserve stock in one service and charge a card in another, each with its own database. There is no single transaction across both. A **saga** splits the operation into local transactions, one per service. If a step fails, earlier steps are undone with **compensating actions**: new transactions with the opposite effect, like releasing the reservation or refunding the charge. Between start and end the system is temporarily inconsistent. This is called **eventual consistency**.
Monolith = one deployable unit. Microservice = independent deploy, own data, one business capability. Start simple, cut by business, expect the network to fail.

At school, a bell rings and everybody knows what to do, though the bell does not talk to anyone one by one. In an **event-driven architecture**, parts of a system announce that something happened, and other parts react. The announcer does not need to know who listens, so the coupling is low.
Event or command?

An **event** is the news of a fact that already happened, so it is named in the past tense: `OrderPlaced`. Its publisher does not send it to anyone in particular. A **command** is a request in the imperative: `PlaceOrder`. It is aimed at one handler, which may accept or refuse it. The difference is in the intent of the message, not in the transport.
Topic or queue?

rows: Every subscriber gets its own copy
Only one of the competing consumers
Telling many parties about the same fact
More reactions to the same event
blocks.caption: Same message, two delivery styles

blocks.text: Delivery guarantees and idempotency

Brokers (the programs that carry messages) often promise **at-least-once delivery**: no message is lost, but some may arrive more than once, for example when the consumer's acknowledgement does not reach the broker. So the consumer must be **idempotent**: processing a message twice must give the same result as once. The usual technique is to store the identifier of every processed event and ignore repeats.

blocks.caption: An idempotent consumer remembers event ids

blocks.text: Order in a partitioned log

Convention: a **partitioned log** such as Apache Kafka. A topic has several partitions, and the message **key** picks the partition. The order guarantee holds **per partition**, not for the whole topic. To keep the events of one account in order (`AccountOpened`, `MoneyDeposited`, `AccountClosed`), give them all the same key, such as the account id, so they go to the same partition. Events of different accounts are processed in parallel with no defined order between them.
Choreography or orchestration?

In a **choreography**, services react to each other's events and none knows the whole flow, like dancers who watch each other. In an **orchestration**, a central coordinator tells each service what to do and in which order, like a conductor. Choreography lowers coupling but makes the flow hard to see and debug. Orchestration keeps the flow visible, at the cost of one component that knows everyone.
The dual-write problem and the outbox

Suppose a program saves an order in the database and then publishes `OrderPlaced` to the broker. These are two systems and two separate steps, so they are not atomic: the program can crash between them, leaving an order that was saved but never announced. The **transactional outbox** pattern fixes it. The event is saved in a table of the same database, in the same transaction as the change of state. A **relay** reads that table and publishes to the broker. Since the relay may publish the same row twice, delivery is at-least-once, and consumers must be idempotent.

blocks.content:
one transaction                  later, in the background
+--------------------+          +-------+       +--------+
| INSERT order       |          | relay | ----> | broker |
| INSERT outbox row  | -------> | reads |       +--------+
+--------------------+          | table |
                                +-------+
blocks.caption: State and event are saved together, then published

blocks.text: CQRS

**CQRS** (Command Query Responsibility Segregation) separates the model that **changes** state (commands) from the model that **reads** it (queries). That is all the pattern requires. Event sourcing, separate databases, messaging and microservices are extra choices that raise the gain in some cases and the cost in all of them. In a simple CRUD (create, read, update, delete), where reads and writes have the same shape, the separation is complexity with no return.

If the read model is updated asynchronously from events, it is **stale** (out of date) for a short time after each write. A user renames a project, the command succeeds, and the list loaded right after still shows the old name. Seconds later it shows the new one. This is the **read-your-own-writes** problem. Common ways out: show the value the command itself returned, send the next read to the write model, or wait until the projection reaches the written version.
At-least-once means duplicates can happen. Every consumer must be idempotent.

Imagine a doctor and a programmer who must build a hospital system. If the doctor says "patient file" and the programmer's code says `Record`, they will misunderstand each other again and again. **Domain-driven design (DDD)**, by Eric Evans, is a way of building software around a deep understanding of the **domain**, the area of business the software is about.

The **ubiquitous language** is the vocabulary that developers and domain experts build together and use everywhere: meetings, documents, tests and code. If the expert says "policy" and the code says `Contract`, every talk needs a translation, and misunderstandings sneak in. The language holds inside one bounded context.
Strategic design: the big map

A **bounded context** is the boundary inside which a model and its words have one single meaning. In an online shop, sales may use "product" for an item with a price and description, and shipping may use "product" for a package with weight and size. Forcing one model for the whole company produces bloated classes and confusing words. DDD accepts **several models**, each consistent in its own context, and makes the links between them explicit.

The **context map** shows how contexts relate and who has power over whom. When you depend on a context that you cannot influence and whose model does not fit yours, such as a legacy billing system, you build an **anti-corruption layer**. It translates between the two models at the border. It costs work to write and maintain, but your new model does not inherit the old problems.

**Strategic design** also splits the domain into **subdomains** and decides where to spend effort. A logistics startup that wins by its route optimisation should put its best people and most careful modelling there.

Needed, but specific to the company and not a differentiator
Works the same in any company (authentication, invoices)
blocks.caption: Where to invest the effort

blocks.text: Tactical design: the pieces inside one context

An **entity** is defined by a continuous **identity**, not by the values of its attributes. A `Customer` can change address and e-mail over the years and is still the same customer, so two entities are compared by their identifier. A **value object** is defined only by its values: it has no identifier, is immutable (never changes after being built) and is compared field by field. `Money` (an amount and a currency) is the classic example. Operations on it return a new object, which avoids side effects when one instance is shared.

An **aggregate** is a group of objects treated as one unit of consistency, with a **root** entity as the only entry point. For an `Order` with its `OrderItem` objects, the root is `Order`. Outside objects hold a reference only to the root, preferably by identifier. Each transaction changes one aggregate, which keeps the rules simple to enforce and the transactions short.

blocks.content:
Aggregate Order
+---------------------------------+
|  Order (root)                   |
|    +-- OrderItem                |
|    +-- OrderItem                |
|    +-- ShippingAddress          |
+---------------------------------+
     ^
     |  only the root is referenced from outside
  Customer (another aggregate, by id)
blocks.caption: One aggregate, one entry point

blocks.text: The **repository** gives the domain the illusion of an in-memory collection of aggregates: add, find by identity, remove. There is **one repository per aggregate root**. The inner objects are loaded and saved with the root, and how many tables are behind it is an implementation detail. If a model has the aggregates `Order` and `Customer`, it has two repositories, even if the data uses four tables.

A **domain service** houses a business operation that is not the natural job of any entity or value object, usually because it involves several of them, like a transfer fee that depends on two accounts. It keeps no state and speaks the ubiquitous language. The **application service** sits one layer above: it coordinates the use case, the transaction and the repositories, with no business rule of its own.

A **domain event** records something relevant to the business that has already happened: order placed, payment confirmed. Because it describes the past, it is immutable and has a past-tense name. Other parts can react to it without the emitter knowing them, which lowers coupling between aggregates and contexts.
Strategic design decides where to invest (contexts, subdomains). Tactical design shapes the inside of one context (entities, value objects, aggregates, repositories).

When you pack a school bag, a big bag holds more but is heavier. There is no perfect bag. In the same way, a well-known saying in architecture is that **there are no best practices, only trade-offs**. Every decision gives something up: more flexibility usually costs more indirection, and more performance usually costs ease of maintenance. A solution is not good or bad in itself, it is suitable or not for a set of requirements and limits. The architect's job is to make explicit what is gained and what is lost.
Keep options open

Robert Martin advises that a good architecture lets you **defer decisions about details**, such as the database or the framework, because the later you decide, the more you know. The **last responsible moment** is the point after which not deciding starts to cost more than deciding. Deferring does not mean doing nothing: it means building so that the detail can be chosen and replaced later. If the team does not yet know how many reads and writes the system will have, hide the database behind a port and choose when the facts arrive.
Two-way doors and one-way doors

Some decisions are like a door you can walk through and come back: a **two-way door**. Choosing a date formatting library, hidden behind a function of your own, is one. A mistake is cheap, so decide fast and learn by trying. Other decisions are a **one-way door**: hard to reverse. The format of the identifiers in a public API used by thousands of clients is one. These deserve analysis, a prototype and a written record. What defines the type is the cost of going back, and good isolation turns many decisions into two-way doors.

The identifier format of a public API
blocks.caption: Spend your analysis effort where going back is costly

blocks.text: Architecture decision records

Years later, nobody remembers why the system is the way it is. An **architecture decision record (ADR)** is a short document that records one architectural decision and the reason for it. Michael Nygard's format has a **title**, a **status** (proposed, accepted, superseded), a **context**, the **decision** and its **consequences**.

blocks.content:
# ADR 7: Use PostgreSQL in the order service
Status: accepted
Context: orders need transactions; we considered MongoDB.
Decision: we will use PostgreSQL.
Consequences: strong consistency (good); harder to scale
writes horizontally (accepted downside).
blocks.caption: A short ADR that shows the exchange

blocks.text: A useful ADR shows the **exchange**: which options were considered, why the others were rejected and which negative consequences the team accepted. A record that lists only advantages is advertising, not documentation. The accepted downsides let someone later notice that the context changed and the decision should be revisited.

ADRs are **append-only**, like a diary. When a decision changes, for example moving from PostgreSQL to another database, you do not edit or delete the old record. You write a new ADR with the new context, and the old one gets the status **superseded**, with a reference to the new one. The history then shows what was known at each moment.

Not every decision needs an ADR. Write one for structurally important decisions that are hard to reverse: the architectural style, the boundaries between modules or services, the persistence model, the protocols between parts. Local decisions that are cheap to undo are already recorded by the code and the commit history. Recording everything buries the decisions that matter.
Overengineering

Layers, ports and dependency inversion are an exchange: they add indirection (extra steps between two things) to make future changes cheaper and to protect the business rules. A script that one person runs once a month, with one implementation of each interface and no plan for another, pays the cost and never gets the benefit. Using every element of clean architecture without need is **overengineering**.

blocks.title: Visualising software architecture with the C4 model (Simon Brown)

blocks.text: Record the hard-to-reverse decisions with their downsides. Keep options open. Do not build flexibility nobody needs.

All these styles answer the same question: how do we keep the rules that matter safe from details that change? Layers cut the program by level. The hexagon and the clean architecture go further and turn the dependencies toward the rules. Microservices apply the same thinking to whole deployments, and events let parts talk without knowing each other. DDD tells you where the boundaries should be, and ADRs remember why you chose them.

blocks.text: Common mistakes

items: Believing that the folder names or the number of circles make an architecture clean. The dependency rule does.
Confusing the order of calls at run time with the direction of imports.
Splitting into services before understanding the domain, and ending with a distributed monolith.
Putting status codes, SQL or framework types inside a use case or an entity.
Using "fast" or "secure" as a requirement without a measurable scenario.
Using events without making consumers idempotent.
Writing an ADR that hides the downsides, or editing an old ADR instead of superseding it.

blocks.text: A good architecture is like a good toy box with labelled compartments. You can swap one toy for another without emptying the whole box, but a box with a hundred tiny compartments for three toys is just a nuisance.
No style is the best for everything. Choose by the requirements, write down what you gave up, and keep the business rules independent from the details.
